objectives: Distinguish radial-velocity vs transit detection methods.
Compute the habitable zone for a star of given luminosity.
Interpret atmospheric biosignatures + their false positives.

slides.title: Exoplanet detection methods
slides.body:
By 2026 we know ~5800 confirmed exoplanets across ~4200 systems. Four primary detection methods, each with biases:

• **Radial velocity** (RV / Doppler): stellar spectral lines wobble by Δv = (M_p/M_*)·v_orb due to the planet pulling the star. Biased toward massive planets close to small stars. Hot Jupiters dominate early surveys (51 Peg b, Mayor + Queloz 1995, Nobel 2019).
• **Transit**: planet crosses stellar disk, drops flux by (R_p/R_*)². Biased toward large planets + edge-on orbits. **Kepler** (2009-2018): ~2700 confirmed planets, statistical census. **TESS** (2018-): brightest stars + best follow-up targets. **JWST**: atmospheric characterization.
• **Direct imaging**: very rare — only works for young, hot, wide-separation planets (HR 8799, β Pic b).
• **Gravitational microlensing**: works for very far / very low-mass planets; statistical only.

Combining methods constrains both **mass** (RV) and **radius** (transit) ⇒ **density**, which constrains composition (gas giant vs rocky vs water world).

slides.title: The habitable zone
slides.body:
**Habitable zone** (HZ): orbital region where surface liquid water can plausibly exist on an Earth-like planet (right atmospheric pressure, sufficient greenhouse, etc.). Approximate inner + outer edges depend on stellar luminosity:

Inner edge (runaway greenhouse, ~Venus): a_HZ_in ≈ √(L/L☉) × 0.95 AU.
Outer edge (CO₂ condensation, ~Mars): a_HZ_out ≈ √(L/L☉) × 1.67 AU.

For the Sun: HZ ≈ 0.95 - 1.67 AU. Earth at 1.0 AU is well within.

For a 0.2 M☉ M dwarf (L ≈ 0.005 L☉): HZ ≈ 0.07 - 0.12 AU — much tighter + closer to the star. Implications: HZ planets are tidally locked + bathed in stellar flares. **TRAPPIST-1** (M8 dwarf, L = 0.0005 L☉): 7 Earth-sized planets, 3-4 in the HZ — but the star erupts violently. Habitability is *plausible* but the radiation environment is hostile.

Habitable ≠ inhabited. Real habitability also depends on planetary mass (atmosphere retention), magnetic field, plate tectonics, water inventory, atmosphere composition, and a stable orbit over Gyrs — none of which we can yet measure remotely.

slides.title: Atmospheric biosignatures + false positives
slides.body:
Robust biosignatures (in principle): atmospheric **O₂ + CH₄** simultaneously, far from chemical equilibrium (Earth: O₂ + CH₄ should react to CO₂ + H₂O in ~10 yr — their coexistence requires a continuous biological source).

Weaker biomarkers: O₃, N₂O, CHCl₃, and the **'red edge'** of vegetation reflectance.

**False positives** (abiotic O₂):
• Photolysis of H₂O in stratosphere + H escape → O₂ buildup (especially for M-dwarf planets with high XUV flux).
• Photolysis of CO₂ → CO + O₂ on dry desert planets.
• Loss of H from runaway-greenhouse early planets.

Mitigation: jointly observe O₂ + CH₄ + N₂; the combination is much harder to explain abiotically.

**JWST** transmission spectroscopy has detected H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, SO₂ in several giant exoplanet atmospheres. For Earth-sized HZ planets (e.g., TRAPPIST-1d, e), JWST is just on the edge of detecting major atmospheric species; biosignature detection awaits future missions (HWO / LUVOIR-class, ARIEL).

The field is currently at the 'precursor' stage: cataloguing atmospheres, ruling out abiotic alternatives, calibrating false-positive rates. A confirmed biosignature detection would likely require *multiple* independent lines of evidence.

question.question: Compute the radial velocity wobble Earth induces on the Sun
question.goal: Estimate the RV signal a Sun-Earth analog system would produce, observed from outside.

steps.prompt: Centre of mass: M_Sun · r_Sun = M_Earth · r_Earth (both measured from the COM). What's the Sun's distance from COM?
The Sun orbits this COM with period 1 yr. What's its orbital speed?
Current best precision of high-resolution spectrographs (ESPRESSO at the VLT)?

acceptedAnswers: ~10 cm/s under ideal conditions; ~30 cm/s realistically. The 9 cm/s 'Earth analog' signal is right at the detection floor — currently inaccessible to any single observation but potentially recoverable with many years of careful monitoring + stellar-activity decorrelation.

steps.reveal: ~10 cm/s under ideal conditions; ~30 cm/s realistically. The 9 cm/s 'Earth analog' signal is right at the detection floor — currently inaccessible to any single observation but potentially recoverable with many years of careful monitoring + stellar-activity decorrelation.

steps.prompt: What does this tell you about the discovery bias toward 'hot Jupiters'?

acceptedAnswers: RV signal scales as M_p × a^(−1/2). A Jupiter-mass planet (300× Earth) at 0.05 AU (50× closer) gives Δv ~ 300 × √20 ≈ 1300× Earth's signal ≈ 120 m/s — easy to detect with 1990s tech. Hot Jupiters dominated early discoveries because they were *easy*, not because they're common. Statistical surveys (Kepler) now show hot Jupiters are < 1% of planetary systems; rocky planets are far more common but harder to detect.

steps.reveal: RV signal scales as M_p × a^(−1/2). A Jupiter-mass planet (300× Earth) at 0.05 AU (50× closer) gives Δv ~ 300 × √20 ≈ 1300× Earth's signal ≈ 120 m/s — easy to detect with 1990s tech. Hot Jupiters dominated early discoveries because they were *easy*, not because they're common. Statistical surveys (Kepler) now show hot Jupiters are < 1% of planetary systems; rocky planets are far more common but harder to detect.

question.question: Why does the transit method preferentially detect planets close to their host stars?
options: Close-in planets have larger physical radii.
Geometric transit probability scales as R_*/a, plus close-in planets have higher orbital frequency (more transits per unit time).
Close-in planets have hotter atmospheres + more pronounced spectroscopic features.
Stellar activity erases transits at large orbital periods.
question.explanation:
Correct. (1) Transit probability ≈ R_*/a — Earth at 1 AU transits the Sun from a randomly oriented observer only ~0.5% of the time; a hot Jupiter at 0.05 AU transits ~10%. (2) Hot Jupiters orbit in days, so a 4-year mission like Kepler sees hundreds of transits; Earth-analogs around Sun-like stars transit once a year, so you need ≥3 years to detect 3 transits. Both effects strongly bias surveys toward close-in planets.

Other options: Close-in planets have larger physical radii.: Hot Jupiters have radii of ~1 R_Jup ≈ Jupiter — no larger than cold gas giants. Radius isn't the issue. | Close-in planets have hotter atmospheres + more pronounced s: True for transmission spectroscopy of *characterization*, not for the initial *detection* of transits. | Stellar activity erases transits at large orbital periods.: Stellar activity adds noise but doesn't preferentially erase transits at large a. The dominant transit biases are geometric + temporal.

hints: Geometry + observation duration both favor short-period planets.
slides.workedSolution: Transit probability = R_* / a (for circular orbits, randomly oriented). Sun-Earth: R☉/AU ≈ 0.005 = 0.5%. So even if every star has an Earth-analog, you'd see transits in only ~1 in 200. Combined with the temporal requirement (≥3 transits for detection ⇒ for Sun-Earth, ≥3 yr baseline), Kepler's confirmed catalog is biased ~100× toward short-period planets. Statistical de-biasing → η_Earth (frequency of Earth-analogs in HZ) ≈ 0.1-0.2 per Sun-like star — surprisingly high.

question.question: JWST transmission spectroscopy of a habitable-zone exoplanet reveals strong CO₂ + H₂O absorption, plus a small amount of O₂. The planet orbits an M dwarf with high XUV flux. Is this strong evidence for life?
options: Yes — O₂ + H₂O together is a classic biosignature.
No — M-dwarf planets can produce abiotic O₂ via H₂O photolysis + H escape; without CH₄ as a co-marker, the signal is ambiguous.
Yes — H₂O is mandatory for life, and we've seen it directly.
No — JWST cannot detect atmospheric species reliably.
question.explanation:
Correct. M dwarfs emit intense XUV that dissociates H₂O → H₂ + O₂ in the upper atmosphere. The H₂ escapes (lighter, easier to lose); O₂ accumulates *abiotically*. So O₂ + H₂O on an M-dwarf planet has a well-known false-positive pathway. To rule it out, you'd want (a) co-existing CH₄ (which O₂ should destroy on a short timescale, so its presence requires continuous source); (b) evidence the planet has been desiccated (water-loss history); (c) absence of CO from CO₂ photolysis. Single biomarker detections on M-dwarf planets must be treated cautiously.

Other options: Yes — O₂ + H₂O together is a classic biosignature.: Premature. The classic biosignature requires O₂ + CH₄ (out of equilibrium); just O₂ + H₂O has well-known abiotic origins, especially around M dwarfs. | Yes — H₂O is mandatory for life, and we've seen it directly.: H₂O alone is not a biosignature — it's common in cold + cool environments throughout the solar system + exoplanet population. Mars + Europa + Enceladus all have H₂O. It's a necessary condition for life-as-we-know-it, not a marker of life. | No — JWST cannot detect atmospheric species reliably.: JWST has reliably detected H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, SO₂, and other species in multiple exoplanet atmospheres since 2022. The question is interpretation, not detection capability.

hints: Think about how O₂ can form without life on M-dwarf planets.
slides.workedSolution: Domagal-Goldman+ 2014 + Meadows+ 2018 catalog the leading abiotic-O₂ pathways: (1) H₂O photolysis + H escape (early in M-dwarf history when XUV is highest, can build up bar-level O₂ over Gyrs); (2) CO₂ photolysis without efficient CO recombination (desert / dry-planet scenario); (3) post-runaway-greenhouse water loss. The 'gold standard' biosignature is the *simultaneous* presence of strongly oxidizing (O₂, O₃) + strongly reducing (CH₄, NH₃) species in chemical disequilibrium — combined with contextual evidence (planetary age, water inventory, host star history). Single-species detections are precursor data; biosignature *claims* require a full atmospheric story.

question.question: Estimate the inner edge of the habitable zone (in AU) for an F5V star with L = 3 L☉. Use a_HZ_in ≈ 0.95 √(L/L☉) AU.

slides.workedSolution: a_HZ_in = 0.95 × √3 = 0.95 × 1.732 ≈ 1.645 AU. The HZ for an F5V star extends from ~1.65 to ~2.9 AU. An Earth analog in this system would need to orbit ~50% farther out than Earth — and the higher UV flux would put more selective pressure on UV-shielding biology.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why finding a 'second Earth' is much harder than just finding a planet of the right size + temperature.
question.rubric: Size + temperature alone don't determine habitability; many other factors matter. Atmospheric composition: too thin (no greenhouse, frozen), too thick (Venus-style runaway), wrong composition (no O₂ if no oxygenic photosynthesis, no CH₄ buffer). Geological activity: plate tectonics + volcanism regulate carbon cycle over Gyrs (Earth's thermostat); without it, climate is unstable. Magnetic field: protects atmosphere from stellar wind stripping (Mars failed; lost atmosphere). Stellar environment: M-dwarf flares strip atmospheres + may sterilize surface; tidally locked planets have extreme weather. Time: life on Earth took ~Gyr to emerge + Gyrs more to oxygenate atmosphere; need stable conditions on those timescales. Biosignatures remotely accessible to us are limited; need both right physics + right chemistry + right history.
